questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, an individual who sells life insurance products without holding the CIIN Certificate of Proficiency is:

opts.x: Permitted to continue for up to 12 months while completing the qualification.
Subject to a fine of up to ₦500,000 per transaction and/or imprisonment for up to 3 years.
Required only to register with NAICOM, without a formal qualification requirement.
Exempt from the qualification requirement if they have more than 5 years' selling experience.

questions.answer: (B) Subject to a fine of up to ₦500,000 per transaction and/or imprisonment for up to 3 years.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 makes unlicensed selling of insurance products a criminal offence with both financial and custodial sanctions. The Cert. COP requirement is a licensing precondition, not a target to work toward while selling. The NAICOM agent licensing framework makes the qualification mandatory before any selling activity commences, and enforcement action can include both a per-transaction fine and imprisonment for serious or persistent violations.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) There is no NIIRA 2025 transitional period allowing unlicensed selling; the Act requires compliance from the date it came into force.
(C) Registration with NAICOM without a qualification is insufficient. The Cert. COP is the statutory minimum qualification, registration without it does not authorise selling.
(D) Years of experience do not substitute for the qualification. NIIRA 2025 removed the pre-existing experience exemption; the Cert. COP is the non-negotiable entry standard.

questions.stem: The fundamental difference between a tied agent and an independent agent in Nigerian life insurance is:

opts.x: Tied agents are employed directly by the insurer; independent agents are self-employed.
Tied agents represent only one insurer; independent agents may place business with multiple insurers.
Tied agents earn first-year commission only; independent agents earn renewal commission as well.
Tied agents are regulated by NAICOM; independent agents are regulated only by the CIIN.

questions.answer: (B) Tied agents represent only one insurer; independent agents may place business with multiple insurers.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The defining legal and commercial distinction is exclusivity. A tied agent has a contractual relationship with one insurer and may only place business with, or on behalf of, that one insurer. An independent agent holds agency agreements with multiple insurers and may advise clients on products from different companies. In Nigeria, the vast majority of agents are tied; the independent agent model is less common and is more closely associated with the broking profession.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Both tied and independent agents are typically self-employed (not directly employed); the employment status distinction is not the defining feature.
(C) Commission structures vary across different agency agreements. Both tied and independent agents can earn renewal commission; this is not the distinguishing characteristic.
(D) Both tied and independent agents are regulated by NAICOM. The CIIN sets qualification standards but does not regulate agents independently of NAICOM.

opts.x: Insurance policies embedded within a life assurance policy as rider benefits.
Life insurance sold exclusively through the insurer's own branch network.
Insurance products integrated seamlessly into the purchase or use of a non-insurance product, such as credit life within a loan disbursement.
Insurance products sold exclusively to formal sector employees through payroll deductions.

questions.answer: (C) Insurance products integrated seamlessly into the purchase or use of a non-insurance product, such as credit life within a loan disbursement.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Embedded insurance is a distribution model in which the insurance product is built into the customer journey of a non-insurance product or service, so that the customer acquires insurance automatically or with minimal friction as part of another transaction. The customer buys a phone on credit → credit life is automatically embedded. A traveller books a flight → travel insurance is embedded at checkout. In Nigeria, the credit life mandate under NIIRA 2025 for qualifying loans is the most commercially significant embedded insurance opportunity.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes rider benefits, supplementary policy features attached to a primary life policy. These are product design features, not a distribution model.
(B) Branch network distribution is a direct proprietary channel, separate from the embedded model where distribution occurs through a non-insurance partner's platform.
(D) Payroll deduction is a premium collection mechanism, often used for group life schemes, not the definition of embedded insurance.

questions.stem: The maximum first-year commission NAICOM regulations permit for an individual life endowment or whole life policy is approximately:

opts.x: 10% of first-year premium.
20% of first-year premium.
40% of first-year premium.
60% of first-year premium.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NAICOM's commission guidelines cap first-year commission on individual life endowment and whole life policies at approximately 40% of the first-year premium. This high first-year commission reflects the significant acquisition effort involved in selling long-duration savings products, agent time, financial needs analysis, underwriting support, and client persuasion. Renewal commissions are significantly lower (typically 5–10% of renewal premium), declining over the policy's life.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) 10% is far below the actual NAICOM cap for long-duration life products and would not adequately compensate agents for the sales effort involved, undermining the distribution model.
(B) 20% is below the actual permitted maximum; the Nigerian market has historically supported high first-year commission rates to incentivise distribution of complex savings products.
(D) 60% exceeds the NAICOM cap. Commission above the prescribed maximum is a market conduct violation under NIIRA 2025.

questions.stem: Under the CBN-NAICOM Joint Regulatory Guidelines on bancassurance, bank staff who sell insurance products are required to:

opts.x: Hold a full CIIN Diploma in Insurance or above.
Hold the CIIN Certificate of Proficiency or an approved equivalent qualification.
Be employed directly by the insurance company, not the bank.
Pass a bank-specific insurance sales assessment designed by the CBN.

questions.answer: (B) Hold the CIIN Certificate of Proficiency or an approved equivalent qualification.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The CBN-NAICOM Joint Regulatory Guidelines on bancassurance require that bank staff who sell insurance products (rather than merely referring customers) must hold the CIIN Cert. COP or an approved equivalent qualification, the same minimum standard required of standalone insurance agents. This ensures that bancassurance customers receive advice from qualified individuals, regardless of whether the distribution channel is the insurer's tied agency network or a bank's branch network.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The CIIN Diploma is a significantly higher qualification than the minimum required for bancassurance selling; the Cert. COP is the mandated minimum, not the Diploma.
(C) Bank staff in a corporate agent bancassurance model remain employees of the bank; they do not transfer employment to the insurer. The bank acts as a corporate agent.
(D) A CBN-designed assessment is not the prescribed qualification. The CIIN Cert. COP is the NAICOM-prescribed standard.

questions.stem:
A life insurer is considering its bancassurance distribution strategy for a new suite of products: a 20-year participating endowment policy; a 5-year term assurance; and a credit life product for mortgage borrowers.
(a) Evaluate the suitability of each product for bancassurance distribution, identifying which products are appropriate for direct teller or relationship manager selling and which may require referral to a specialist agent.
(b) Describe the training and qualification requirements that bank staff must meet before selling these products.
(c) Explain the consumer protection risks in bancassurance distribution and the NIIRA 2025 and CBN-NAICOM framework provisions that manage them.
(d) Describe the premium remittance obligations of the bank as a corporate agent.

model.h: Part (a): Product Suitability for Bancassurance

rows: SPECIALIST REFERRAL REQUIRED. This is a complex, long-duration product with significant premium commitment (typically ₦100,000–₦500,000+ per year), participation in with-profit bonuses, and surrender value implications that require detailed explanation. The customer needs a proper financial needs analysis and benefit illustration review, not a quick teller counter transaction. Bank relationship managers with Cert. COP may introduce the product and gather information, but the full suitability assessment and sale should be completed by a specialist life insurance adviser.

APPROPRIATE FOR DIRECT BANCASSURANCE SALE. A 5-year term policy is simpler: fixed premium, fixed benefit, no savings element, no surrender value complexity. A bank relationship manager with Cert. COP can explain the product, assess suitability (income level, dependants, existing cover), and complete the application. The product is well-suited to the bancassurance interaction moment, e.g., when a customer opens a new salary account or takes a personal loan.

HIGHEST BANCASSURANCE SUITABILITY. The credit life product is the definitive embedded bancassurance product; it is naturally triggered at mortgage origination, has a straightforward declining benefit matching the mortgage balance, and the customer has a legal obligation to hold it under NIIRA 2025. The bank's mortgage team can integrate credit life into the mortgage disbursement workflow with minimal separate selling effort.

model.h: Part (b): Training and Qualification Requirements

For bank staff selling directly (not just referring):
• Minimum qualification: CIIN Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP), required by NAICOM and the CBN-NAICOM Joint Guidelines.
• Product-specific training: All staff selling any specific product must complete the insurer's product training programme for that product, covering benefit structure, pricing basis, suitability criteria, policy conditions, and exclusions.
• Benefit illustration training: Staff must be able to present and explain the standardised NAICOM-compliant benefit illustration for each product accurately.
• AML/KYC training: Staff must complete AML training (MLPPA 2022 requirements apply to insurance as well as banking).
• Annual CPD: Ongoing professional development required to maintain qualification currency and product knowledge.
Part (c): Consumer Protection Risks and Regulatory Framework

Key consumer protection risks in bancassurance:
1. Mis-selling through misunderstanding: Bank staff whose primary training is in banking products may inadequately understand insurance product features, exclusions, or the implications of early surrender, leading to inaccurate presentations.
2. Pressure selling: The bank's established customer relationship and the power dynamic between bank staff and customers can create coercive pressure to purchase insurance products that may not be suitable.
3. Bundling without consent: Quietly embedding insurance within banking products without explicit customer consent is a regulatory violation.

NIIRA 2025 and CBN-NAICOM framework responses:
• Mandatory Cert. COP requirement ensures a minimum competency standard.
• Benefit illustration obligation; the customer must receive a plain language benefit illustration before purchase.
• Cooling-off right (21 days); the customer can cancel without penalty after receiving the policy document.
• The CBN-NAICOM Guidelines prohibit conditioning banking products on insurance purchase.
• NAICOM's TCF framework requires that each sale is suitable for the individual customer.
Part (d): Premium Remittance Obligations

As a licensed corporate agent, the bank's premium remittance obligations include:
1. Premium Trust Account: All client insurance premiums collected must be held in a segregated Premium Trust Account, separate from the bank's own operating accounts. This is a regulatory requirement under NIIRA 2025 and the CBN-NAICOM Guidelines.
2. Remittance timeline: Premiums must be remitted to the insurer within the timeframe specified in the corporate agency agreement, typically 5–15 business days of collection. Late remittance is a breach of the agreement and a market conduct violation.
3. No premium finance: The bank cannot use collected premiums to finance its own operations, even temporarily. The trust account is ringfenced.
4. Reconciliation reporting: Monthly reconciliation of premium collection against policy issuance must be provided to the insurer, enabling the insurer to verify that all premiums collected have been remitted and applied to valid policies.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer’s tied agency force of 3,000 agents generates ₦120 billion in first-year premium annually. However, the 13-month persistency rate has declined from 72% three years ago to 56% currently.
(a) Calculate the approximate annual premium ‘lost’ from the 16-percentage-point decline in persistency, assuming the in-force book is ₦500bn and the average renewal premium is 90% of first-year premium.
(b) Identify three structural causes of declining persistency in a Nigerian tied agency force.
(c) Describe three commission structure modifications or distribution management interventions that could improve persistency.
(d) Explain how the NIIRA 2025 agent licensing and CPD requirements might contribute to improved persistency over the medium term.

model.h: Part (a): Annual Premium Lost from Persistency Decline

At 72% persistency, the policies lapsing annually: 28% × ₦500bn = ₦140bn of in-force book.
At 56% persistency, the policies lapsing annually: 44% × ₦500bn = ₦220bn of in-force book.

Additional lapses from the persistency decline: ₦220bn − ₦140bn = ₦80bn of additional lapsed sum assured.

Annual premium income lost from the additional lapses (at 90% renewal premium rate on the additional lapsed SA):
Additional lapsed premium income: ₦80bn × (average renewal premium rate). Assuming average renewal premium is 2% of sum assured: ₦80bn × 2% × 90% = ₦1.44bn additional annual premium lost from the 16-point persistency decline.

Note for candidates: The exact calculation depends on the average premium rate assumption. The examiner is testing the logical approach; the answer should demonstrate that the premium loss = (change in lapse rate) × (in-force book) × (average renewal premium rate). Full credit for a correctly structured calculation with stated assumptions.
Part (b): Three Structural Causes of Declining Persistency

1. Commission-driven mis-selling: Agents maximising first-year commission sell policies to customers who cannot sustain the premiums, particularly if first-year commission is high relative to renewal commission (the 'churning incentive'). Policies sold to financially marginal customers predictably lapse in year 1–2.

2. Agent attrition and orphan policies: In a tied agency force of 3,000, agent turnover may be 30–50% per year in a poorly managed force. When an agent leaves, their policy book becomes 'orphan', no active relationship with the policyholder. Without an agent maintaining the relationship and reminding policyholders of premium due dates, lapse rates among orphan policies are typically 2–3× higher than among serviced portfolios.

3. Macroeconomic income disruption: Premium commitment cannot be sustained through income shocks. A customer paying ₦120,000/year on a life policy who loses their job, or whose naira income is eroded by 40% inflation, will prioritise food and rent over insurance. Persistency declines are typically correlated with Nigerian macroeconomic volatility.
Part (c): Three Interventions to Improve Persistency

1. Persistency-linked commission clawback: Restructure commission so that if a policy lapses within 24 months, the agent is required to repay a defined proportion of the first-year commission. This directly aligns the agent's financial interest with long-term policy persistency, agents will be more careful about selling to customers who cannot sustain premiums if they face financial consequences from early lapses.

2. Orphan policy management programme: Create a dedicated orphan policy team, agents or customer service specialists who proactively contact policyholders whose agents have left, conduct policyholder welfare reviews, and offer policy servicing support. Evidence from other markets shows that active orphan management can improve orphan persistency by 10–15 percentage points.

3. Pre-lapse intervention workflow: Use data analytics to identify policies at risk of lapse before the premium falls due, high-risk indicators include: first missed premium; no digital engagement in 6 months; agent inactive. Trigger a proactive outreach programme (call, WhatsApp, SMS, agent visit) 30–60 days before the grace period expires, offering options including premium holiday, paid-up conversion, or a conservation call. Studies show that proactive conservation reduces lapse rates by 20–30% among at-risk policies.
Part (d): NIIRA 2025 Agent Licensing and CPD Impact on Persistency

NIIRA 2025's agent licensing and CPD framework will contribute to persistency improvement over the medium term through three mechanisms:

1. Quality improvement through qualification: The mandatory Cert. COP requirement raises the professional floor for all selling agents. A better-qualified agent understands product features, suitability requirements, and benefit illustrations more deeply, reducing the probability of selling unsuitable products to customers who will predictably lapse.

2. CPD requirement sustaining professional standards: The annual CPD obligation ensures that agents' product knowledge and sales practices are continuously updated. An agent who is required to demonstrate current competency every year is less likely to rely on outdated or misleading product descriptions that lead to customer disappointment and lapse.

3. Reduced market of unlicensed sellers: NIIRA 2025's enforcement against unlicensed selling will remove the lowest-quality, most exploitative agents from the market, the cohort most associated with mis-selling and high lapse rates. A smaller, better-qualified agency force should produce structurally better persistency.

questions.stem:
A microfinance bank (MFB) operating in a tier-2 Nigerian city (population approximately 300,000) with a loan portfolio of 15,000 active borrowers wants to enter a distribution partnership with a microinsurance-licensed life insurer.
(a) Describe the regulatory steps the MFB must take to become a licensed corporate agent for the insurer.
(b) Identify three microinsurance products appropriate for MFB distribution and explain the design features that make each suitable for the MFB’s customer base.
(c) Explain how premiums would be collected and remitted under the partnership arrangement.
(d) Describe two challenges the insurer should anticipate in managing this distribution relationship and how each should be addressed in the corporate agency agreement.

model.h: Part (a): Regulatory Steps for MFB to Become Licensed Corporate Agent

Step 1: NAICOM application: The MFB submits a corporate agent licence application to NAICOM, enclosing: certificate of incorporation; CAC registration; CBN microfinance bank licence; board resolution authorising the insurance distribution activity; list of designated insurance sales staff.

Step 2: NIIRA 2025 compliance review: NAICOM reviews whether the MFB meets the corporate agent requirements: minimum capital (the MFB's existing capital must meet NAICOM's corporate agent minimum); no outstanding regulatory sanctions; corporate governance documentation.

Step 3: Staff qualification verification: Confirmation that all designated MFB staff who will sell or advise on insurance products hold the CIIN Cert. COP or an approved equivalent.

Step 4: NAICOM licence issuance: On successful review, NAICOM issues the corporate agent certificate, specifying: the classes of insurance the MFB is authorised to distribute; the insurer(s) with whom the corporate agency agreement has been filed.

Step 5: Corporate agency agreement registration: The signed Master Distribution Agreement between the MFB and the life insurer must be filed with and acknowledged by NAICOM before any insurance sales commence.
Part (b): Three Appropriate Microinsurance Products and Design Features

rows: Design Features Making It Suitable for MFB Distribution
Credit life insurance (mandatory under NIIRA 2025 for qualifying loans)

Automatically embedded at loan disbursement, no separate selling required. Reducing sum assured mirroring the loan balance. Single premium collected at loan origination, bundled into the loan amount. Simple underwriting, no medical evidence required below defined limits. The MFB's 15,000 borrowers represent an automatic qualifying market.

A group policy covering all MFB borrowers for a fixed death benefit (e.g., ₦500,000 – ₦2m) regardless of loan balance. Annual premium collected via the borrower's regular contribution to the MFB. Simple flat benefit avoids the reducing-balance calculation complexity. Provides death protection beyond the loan balance, a genuine additional value proposition for borrowers' families.

A simple whole life or endowment product with weekly/monthly premiums as low as ₦500. Premiums collected via the MFB's existing mobile banking and USSD collection infrastructure, no new payment infrastructure required. Policy issuance and premium tracking automated through API integration. Claims paid via mobile money, no branch visit required. Designed to be sold by the MFB's loan officers in the field during borrower visits.

model.h: Part (c): Premium Collection and Remittance

Collection mechanisms:
• Credit life: Single premium deducted from loan disbursement proceeds at drawdown; the premium is remitted to the insurer on the same day as disbursement.
• Group life: Annual group premium paid by the MFB from its own funds (covered by a markup in the borrower's annual account fee) and remitted to the insurer.
• Savings-linked product: Weekly/monthly premiums collected via the MFB's USSD or mobile banking system, aggregated daily, and remitted to the insurer via API-triggered batch transfer.

Premium Trust Account:
All collected premiums must be held in a segregated Premium Trust Account maintained by the MFB as corporate agent, separate from the MFB's operating accounts. The corporate agency agreement should specify: the bank holding the trust account; dual-signatory requirements for withdrawals; and the remittance timetable (typically within 3–5 business days of collection for digital premium streams).
Part (d): Two Challenges and Agreement Provisions

Challenge 1: MFB staff capacity and turnover:
MFBs typically have high staff turnover and limited insurance product knowledge. Staff trained today may leave within 6–12 months, leaving the distribution channel without qualified sellers.
Agreement provision: Include a training obligation clause requiring the MFB to maintain a minimum percentage of Cert. COP-qualified staff (e.g., at least one per branch). The insurer should provide initial training free of charge and ongoing train-the-trainer support. Staff departure must be notified to the insurer within 5 days so replacement training can be arranged.

Challenge 2: Premium remittance reliability:
MFBs in tier-2 cities may face liquidity pressures that create temptation to delay premium remittance, using insurance premiums as short-term working capital.
Agreement provision: Require the MFB to maintain a minimum Premium Trust Account balance, with daily reconciliation reports provided to the insurer. Include a right of audit for the insurer over the trust account. Specify automatic late-remittance penalties (interest at CBN minimum rediscount rate on delayed amounts). Include a right to terminate the corporate agency agreement with 14 days' notice for any remittance default exceeding 15 days.

questions.stem: The distribution model that will define the Nigerian life insurance market’s growth trajectory over the next decade is not the traditional tied agency but a combination of digitally-enabled agency, bancassurance, and embedded digital distribution. Critically evaluate this proposition. In your answer: assess the current relative contribution of each major distribution channel to Nigerian life premium income; analyse the structural advantages and limitations of each channel for different market segments and product types; evaluate the NIIRA 2025 regulatory changes (particularly agent licensing and the Insurtech Guidelines) as enablers or constraints on channel innovation; and propose a channel mix evolution strategy for a mid-size Nigerian life insurer seeking to double its premium income over five years.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition correctly identifies the directional shift in Nigerian insurance distribution but is too absolute: the traditional tied agency will not disappear; it will evolve. The market will not be won by a single channel but by the insurer that most effectively deploys multiple channels in a segment-specific, product-appropriate architecture.
Current Channel Contributions

The tied retail agency force continues to generate the dominant share of individual life premium income, estimated at 65–75% of total individual life AFYP. Bancassurance accounts for approximately 15–20% of total life premium (primarily through group schemes and savings products). Direct and digital channels collectively account for less than 10%, though this is growing rapidly. Embedded insurance is nascent but growing quickly through credit life mandates.

This distribution reflects the market's history; the agency model was built over decades; digital channels are 2–5 years old in any serious form. The question is trajectory, not current snapshot.
Structural Advantages and Limitations by Channel

Digitally-enabled agency: Advantages: The agent relationship retains its trust-building value for complex products (money-back, endowment, keyman) where a human conversation is required. Digital tools (agent app, e-proposal, WhatsApp) reduce the administrative burden and improve data quality. Limitations: Agent attrition remains high; digital enablement does not fix the underlying incentive misalignment that drives mis-selling and poor persistency.

Bancassurance: Advantages: Immediate access to the bank's existing customer base with established trust; natural product integration moments (salary account → life cover; mortgage → credit life). Limitations: Bank staff sell banking products primarily; insurance is secondary. Staff turnover and training quality challenges. The product shelf must be narrow and simple to enable non-specialist selling.

Embedded digital: Advantages: Near-frictionless distribution at scale; reaches segments the agent and bank branch cannot. The credit life mandate creates a massive embedded market. Limitations: Products must be extremely simple; customer awareness of insurance purchase may be low (leading to disputes at claims); trust is borrowed from the digital platform partner, not earned by the insurer.
NIIRA 2025 Regulatory Changes as Enablers and Constraints

Enablers: The NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines 2025 create formal Partnering and Standalone Insurtech tracks, providing regulatory clarity for fintech, agritech, and digital platform partnerships that were previously operating in a grey zone. The embedded credit life mandate creates a compulsory market for embedded insurance at scale.

Constraints: The Cert. COP requirement for all sellers in digital and embedded channels creates a compliance challenge, a digital distribution partner (an e-commerce platform or USSD service) that employs thousands of agents-equivalent must ensure each qualified seller meets the standard. The data protection framework (NDPA 2023) requires explicit consent and data processing agreements for all digital lead generation activities, adding friction to large-scale digital marketing.
Channel Mix Evolution Strategy for a Mid-Size Insurer

Year 1: Digitally enable the existing agency force (defensive): Deploy an agent app for e-proposals, digital client files, and premium remittance confirmation. Reduce orphan lapse rates by 15 points through proactive digital contact. Target: +₦5bn AFYP from productivity improvement in existing force.

Year 2–3: Launch bancassurance partnerships (offensive growth): Partner with 2 commercial banks and 3 MFBs. Develop a three-product shelf (credit life; simple term; education endowment). Invest in branch-level training. Target: +₦15bn AFYP from bancassurance.

Year 3–4: Embedded insurance partnerships (scale): Integrate credit life API with 2 fintech lenders. Partner with one agritech platform for crop-linked death benefit products. Target: +₦10bn AFYP from embedded channels.

Year 4–5: Digital direct (brand investment): Launch USSD-accessible term assurance product. Invest in digital marketing (Instagram, WhatsApp) targeting urban millennials. Claims storytelling content marketing. Target: +₦8bn AFYP from direct digital.

Total: ₦38bn additional AFYP over five years, a doubling of a mid-size insurer with ₦30–35bn current AFYP.

questions.stem: ‘Commission-based distribution is the original sin of the Nigerian life insurance market: it creates structural incentives for mis-selling, drives up product cost, rewards volume over quality, and produces the high early-lapse rates that destroy both profitability and policyholder trust.’ Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to the Nigerian life insurance distribution environment. In your answer: analyse the evidence for and against commission-based distribution as a driver of mis-selling and poor persistency in Nigeria; assess whether NIIRA 2025’s disclosure, licensing, and conduct requirements are adequate to manage the conflicts of interest inherent in commission-driven distribution; evaluate the commercial and practical feasibility of fee-based advisory distribution as an alternative for different market segments; and identify the governance and management controls insurers should implement to harness the productivity of commission-based distribution while managing its market conduct risks.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition identifies a real structural problem with substantial evidence supporting it, but overstates the case. Commission-based distribution is not inherently sinful; it is the design and governance of commission structures that determines whether they serve or undermine the market. The appropriate response is not abolition of commission (which is commercially impractical in a market with Nigeria's characteristics) but redesign, governance, and regulatory oversight.
Evidence For: Commission as Driver of Market Pathology

1. High early-lapse rates: The correlation between front-loaded commission structures (40% first-year, 5% renewal) and high early-year lapse rates (18% year-1, 10% year-2 in many Nigerian portfolios) is structural. The agent who earns ₦40,000 commission on a ₦100,000 first-year premium has no financial incentive to ensure the customer can sustain the premium; the commission is earned at sale, not at renewal.

2. Churning: Agents who encourage existing policyholders to surrender and repurchase, generating a fresh first-year commission, at the expense of the policyholder who loses surrender value and resets their coverage. Churning is well-documented in the Nigerian market.

3. Product cost elevation: Commission costs are embedded in the gross premium. Products with 40% first-year commission necessarily have a higher gross premium for equivalent net coverage than products with lower commission. This makes Nigerian life insurance structurally less price-competitive than it should be.

4. Mis-selling to marginal buyers: The commission incentive drives selling to customers who cannot sustain the premiums, because the commission is paid regardless. These policies predictably lapse early, harming policyholders and damaging industry trust.
Evidence Against: Commission's Positive Functions

1. Enables distribution reach: Nigeria's life insurance penetration is below 0.5% of GDP. The commission model, in which the distribution cost is paid only when a sale is made, enables the deployment of tens of thousands of agents without upfront fixed salary cost. A fee-based model requires customers to pay for advice regardless of purchase, which most Nigerians will not do.

2. Income distribution: Commission payments support the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of agents, many of whom are micro-entrepreneurs in communities where formal employment is scarce. The commission model is a significant informal sector income mechanism.

3. Sales productivity: Commission-based motivation produces higher sales volumes than salaried salesforces in most market contexts, particularly in challenging segments where rejection rates are high and persistence is required.
NIIRA 2025 Adequacy in Managing Conflicts of Interest

NIIRA 2025 addresses commission-related conflicts through: mandatory disclosure of commission to clients; Cert. COP qualification requirements reducing the most unsophisticated mis-selling; TCF principle requiring suitability assessment before sale; the s.62 statutory commission caps (group life 9%, single-premium annuity 3%) and NAICOM guidelines on first-year loading.

Adequacy assessment: These provisions are necessary but not sufficient. Disclosure of commission is only effective if the client understands what it means and can use the information, financial literacy is required that many Nigerian policyholders do not possess. The TCF principle is difficult to enforce at scale without customer-outcome monitoring data that NAICOM does not yet systematically collect.
Feasibility of Fee-Based Distribution

Fee-based advisory models are commercially feasible for:
• High-net-worth individuals who purchase complex financial products (keyman insurance, retirement planning, executive benefit design), where the fee is proportionate to the product complexity and the client's sophistication.
• Corporate clients purchasing group life, group health, and employee benefit programmes, where a broker's advisory fee is standard.

Fee-based models are NOT commercially feasible for:
• Mass-market individual life insurance in Nigeria's informal sector, a customer buying a ₦500/week micro-life product cannot pay an additional advisory fee.
• Any segment where the financial literacy to value and pay for advice has not been developed.
Governance and Management Controls

1. Persistency-weighted commission design: Structure commission so that a significant portion (30–40%) is paid over the first 3 years of the policy's life rather than entirely in year 1. An agent who receives ₦12,000 in year 1 and ₦9,000 in year 2 (contingent on the policy remaining in force) has a direct financial interest in persistency.

2. Mandatory suitability documentation: Require agents to complete a documented suitability assessment for every individual life policy, confirming that the product is appropriate for the customer's income, risk profile, and financial goals. Random audit of suitability records creates compliance accountability.

3. Commission clawback: Require agents to repay commission on policies that lapse within 24 months of issue, except where lapse is attributable to documented income disruption rather than mis-selling.

4. Agency manager quality accountability: Align agency manager (Unit Manager) overrider commission to persistency metrics, not just to new business volume. A Unit Manager whose team's persistency is below 65% should earn reduced overriders, creating a direct managerial incentive to manage persistency actively.
